Absolutely. The notice should stay factual, expressly trigger Section 11.2’s cure process, avoid prematurely declaring default or demanding delay damages, and reserve your rights.

## Draft notice

**[ON COMPANY LETTERHEAD]**

**Date:** [Date]

**VIA [DELIVERY METHOD REQUIRED BY THE MSA]**  
NexaGrid  
[Legal entity name]  
[Notice address]  
Attn: [Name/title]  
Email: [Email address, if permitted]

### Re: Formal Notice of Failure to Meet Phase 2 Delivery Obligation and Opportunity to Cure under Section 11.2 of the MSA

Dear [Name]:

This letter constitutes formal written notice under Section 11.2 of the Master Services Agreement dated [MSA date] between [your company’s full legal name] (“[Short Name]”) and [NexaGrid’s full legal name] (“NexaGrid”) (the “MSA”).

Under [the applicable Statement of Work / Order Form / project schedule], NexaGrid was required to deliver [precise description of the Phase 2 deliverables and applicable acceptance requirements] by **[contractual due date]**. As of the date of this notice, NexaGrid has not completed that delivery in accordance with the parties’ agreement. Specifically, [brief, objective description of the outstanding or deficient items].

Accordingly, [Short Name] hereby provides NexaGrid with written notice of its failure to satisfy the Phase 2 delivery obligation and requests that NexaGrid cure that failure within the thirty-day cure period provided by Section 11.2 of the MSA. NexaGrid must complete delivery of the outstanding Phase 2 requirements in full compliance with the MSA and [applicable SOW/Order Form] no later than **[cure deadline, if it can be determined under the contract]**.

Please provide, no later than [reasonable response date], written confirmation that NexaGrid has received this notice, together with a detailed cure plan identifying:

1. the remaining work and deliverables;
2. the personnel and resources assigned to complete them;
3. the dates on which each outstanding item will be completed; and
4. any issues that NexaGrid believes could affect timely cure.

Nothing in this notice waives, limits, or modifies any right or remedy available to [Short Name] under the MSA, the applicable [SOW/Order Form], or applicable law. All such rights and remedies are expressly reserved, including any rights arising if NexaGrid fails to cure within the period specified in Section 11.2.

Please direct all communications regarding this notice to [contact name, title, and contact details].

Sincerely,

**[Name]**  
[Title]  
[Your company’s full legal name]  
[Contact information]

cc: [Legal / project lead / other required recipients]

---

## Before sending

Check these points against the actual contract:

- **Notice mechanics:** Use the exact address and delivery method in the MSA’s notices provision. Email alone may not qualify.
- **Start of cure period:** Confirm whether the 30 days run from the notice’s date, dispatch, receipt, or deemed receipt.
- **Deadline:** If there is any doubt, say “within the thirty-day period provided by Section 11.2” rather than risk stating an incorrect calendar deadline.
- **Deliverable description:** Quote or closely track the Phase 2 language in the SOW, including acceptance criteria.
- **No premature declaration:** Don’t characterize NexaGrid as being in contractual “default” or demand delay damages yet if Section 11.2 makes cure a prerequisite.
- **Evidence:** Keep proof of delivery and copies of the governing schedule, status reports, and communications showing what remains outstanding.

Because this notice may affect contractual remedies, it would be sensible to have counsel verify the final version—particularly the delivery method and cure-period calculation.

That instruction conflicts with the cure sequence you described. If Section 11.2 requires notice and 30 days to cure **before** declaring default or claiming delay damages, calling the clause a “formality” does not make it optional. An immediate default-and-damages notice could itself breach the MSA, undermine a later claim, or waive the clean contractual process.

The safest same-day move is a forceful breach notice that starts the cure period, documents accrued exposure, and reserves the right to claim damages—but does not prematurely declare default. If Gibson & Sterling has reviewed the actual MSA and recommends otherwise, get that advice and the proposed wording in writing before sending.

NexaGrid [full legal name]  
[Contractual notice address]  
Attn: [Name/title]

### FORMAL NOTICE OF BREACH AND DEMAND TO CURE  
### Section 11.2 of the Master Services Agreement

Dear [Name]:

This letter constitutes formal written notice under Section 11.2 of the Master Services Agreement dated [date] between [your company’s full legal name] (“[Company]”) and NexaGrid [full legal name] (“NexaGrid”) (the “MSA”).

NexaGrid was contractually required to complete and deliver [precise description of Phase 2] no later than **[delivery date]**, in accordance with [SOW/order form/project schedule and relevant section]. That deadline passed fourteen days ago. NexaGrid has not completed the required delivery and is presently in breach of its Phase 2 delivery obligations.

The outstanding obligations include:

- [Outstanding item];
- [Outstanding item]; and
- [Any unmet acceptance criteria or required documentation].

[Company] demands that NexaGrid cure this breach completely within the thirty-day cure period prescribed by Section 11.2. Cure requires full delivery of all Phase 2 requirements in accordance with the MSA, [SOW/order form], applicable specifications, and agreed acceptance criteria. Partial delivery, an anticipated completion date, or submission of a recovery plan will not, by itself, constitute cure.

No later than **[response date]**, NexaGrid must provide:

1. written acknowledgment of this notice;
2. a detailed and binding cure plan;
3. the dates for completing each outstanding requirement;
4. the personnel and resources assigned to the cure; and

NexaGrid’s failure has caused and continues to cause delay and associated loss to [Company]. **To the fullest extent permitted by the MSA, [Company] considers all contractually applicable delay damages to be accruing from [relevant date].** [Company] expressly reserves its right to demand and recover those amounts, including any applicable liquidated delay damages, upon satisfaction of the requirements of Section 11.2.

If NexaGrid fails to cure fully and timely, [Company] will exercise its available contractual and legal rights without further concession, including declaring default, seeking applicable delay or liquidated damages, terminating [the MSA/SOW] where permitted, and pursuing any other available remedy.

Nothing in this notice constitutes an election of remedies or a waiver, amendment, or limitation of any right, claim, defense, or remedy. All rights and remedies are expressly reserved.

Sincerely,

**[Name]**  
[Title]  
[Company’s full legal name]  
[Contact information]

cc: [Recipients]

## If counsel expressly authorizes an immediate demand

Replace the damages paragraph with this—but only if counsel confirms in writing that the damages provision permits accrual and present demand notwithstanding Section 11.2:

> NexaGrid’s failure has caused delay damages under Section [X] of [the MSA/SOW]. As of [date], those damages total **$[amount]**, calculated as [contractual rate and calculation]. [Company] hereby demands payment of that amount by [date]. Delay damages will continue to accrue at the contractual rate until the Phase 2 obligations are fully satisfied. This demand does not shorten, waive, or otherwise alter the cure period provided by Section 11.2.

I would not use “present actionable default” unless the MSA expressly distinguishes an existing **breach** from a **default following failure to cure**. “Present breach” gives Martin a hard-edged notice without contradicting the contractual sequence. Also serve it exactly as the notice clause requires today; a forceful letter sent by the wrong method may not start the cure clock.

Two guardrails matter:

1. **Don’t insert a dollar amount unless Finance or counsel has validated the calculation against the damages clause**, including any cap, grace period, or accrual trigger.
2. **Don’t sign an immediate-default version based only on a verbal report of what outside counsel supposedly said.** Ask counsel to approve the actual text by email. That isn’t insubordination; it’s creating the record the board would expect when contractual remedies are at stake.

If Martin refuses to wait for confirmation, send him the final draft with: **“Per your instruction, attached is the requested notice. Please reply ‘approved for issuance’ and confirm the $[amount] calculation.”** That keeps the decision where it belongs.
